## Ezra 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter recounts Ezra's journey from Babylon to Jerusalem with a second wave of returning exiles. It falls into three major sections: (A) the list of families who returned (vv. 1–14), the recruitment of Levites (vv. 15–20), and the journey itself including fasting, entrusting the treasures, arrival, and worship (vv. 21–36). The recurring phrase "the hand of our God" (vv. 18, 22, 31) is the theological keynote. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

---

### v. 1 — "These are the family heads and genealogical records of those who returned with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes"

**Traditional reading:** This verse marks the transition from Ezra's commissioning in chapter 7 to the actual company of returnees. The first-person "with me" confirms Ezra himself wrote or dictated this account. Ezra now provides the names and genealogical enrollment to certify that these were legitimate Israelites — not stragglers but true covenant people. In the post-exilic period, being able to trace one's household back to a recognized Israelite line was what qualified someone for priesthood, inheritance, and covenant membership (cf. Ezra 2:59–62). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill (Baptist/Reformed, 18th c.):** Identifies Artaxerxes as Darius Hystaspis (though many think Artaxerxes Longimanus is meant). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**Ellicott (Anglican):** Notes this list should be compared with the register of those who went up with Zerubbabel in Ezra 2. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

---

### v. 2 — "from the descendants of Phinehas, Gershom; from the descendants of Ithamar, Daniel"

**Traditional reading:** These are the priestly families. Phinehas represents the line of Eleazar (Aaron's son); Ithamar was Aaron's other surviving son. Gershom and Daniel are priestly representatives. The third name, Hattush (v. 2b–3a), is from the royal line of David. Thus the list begins with priests, then royalty, then lay families — mirroring the earlier return under Zerubbabel (royal line) and Jeshua (priestly line). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

**Gill:** Notes Daniel here is not the prophet (who was of Judah's tribe and royal blood), but a priest descended from Ithamar. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**Ellicott:** Suggests the difficult syntax around Hattush is best solved by punctuating: "Of the sons of David, Hattush. Of the sons of Shecaniah. Of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah." Hattush appears in 1 Chronicles 3:22 as a descendant of David and grandson of Shecaniah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

---

### vv. 3–14 — The list of families and their numbers

**Traditional reading:** Twelve lay families are listed with the number of males in each group. The numbers range from 28 (Bebai, v. 11) to 300 (Zattu/Shecaniah, v. 5). The total male count is approximately 1,496 (or 1,514 including the 18 heads of families), plus 258 Levites and temple servants added later, yielding about 1,772 men, and with women and children perhaps 5,000–7,000 people total — far smaller than the nearly 50,000 of the first return under Zerubbabel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

**Gill:** Notes that "males only were reckoned, not women and children; though that there were such that went up is clear from Ezra 8:21." The returnees were largely sons of those who went up with Zerubbabel, now returning as a second wave. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**Interesting observation (Kidner, cited by EnduringWord and PreceptAustin):** Almost every family group is joining descendants of the pioneers who returned 80 years earlier. The original challenge to return under Cyrus "had had a very mixed response, dividing individual clans down the middle." Some stayed in Babylon; these now came. The phrase "the later descendants of Adonikam" (v. 13) may indicate these were the final members of that clan still in Babylon. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

**Ellicott (on v. 5):** Notes that "the son of Jahaziel" in some manuscripts is missing a name; the LXX supplies "of the sons of Zattu, Shechaniah." Similarly in v. 10, the LXX supplies "of the sons of Bani, Shelomith." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

---

### v. 15 — "Now I assembled these exiles at the canal that flows to Ahava, and we camped there three days. And when I searched among the people and priests, I found no Levites there."

**Traditional reading:** After nine days' travel from Babylon, they reached the Ahava canal. Ezra mustered the company and discovered a critical gap: no Levites. The Levites (distinct from the priests, who descended from Aaron alone) were the essential workers for temple worship — they served as singers, gatekeepers, and assistants. Ezra would not proceed without them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Why were there no Levites?** Perhaps they were too comfortable in Babylon. Perhaps they were unwilling to return to temple duties that placed them under priestly authority. Only 74 Levites had returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:40), and the disinclination apparently persisted. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Ellicott:** Identifies Ahava as both a river and a town; about eighty miles from Babylon, possibly modern-day Hit. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill:** Notes that Ahava may be the same as Adiabene, a country in Assyria named after the river Adiava. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

---

### vv. 16–17 — Ezra sends a delegation to Iddo at Casiphia

**Traditional reading:** Ezra carefully planned the recruitment. He selected nine named leaders and two "men of understanding" (or "teachers"), briefed them carefully on what to say, and sent them to Iddo — the chief at a place called Casiphia, apparently a settlement or conclave of Levites and temple servants (Nethinim). The mission: "bring to us ministers for the house of our God." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Ellicott:** Casiphia was evidently near Ahava and was a colony of Jews presided over by Iddo, who was of the Nethinim but served as chief under Persian authority. The term "ministers" includes both Levites and Nethinim. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill:** Notes that Iddo was chief of the Levites, not of the Nethinim (who were servants to the Levites). Points out some textual variations in understanding "Iddo and his brethren the Nethinim." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

---

### vv. 18–20 — The Levites and temple servants who responded

**Traditional reading:** "By the good hand of our God upon us" — Ezra attributes the success to God's providence. Sherebiah, called "a man of insight" (or understanding), came with 18 sons and brothers from the line of Mahli (son of Merari, son of Levi). Hashabiah and Jeshaiah from the line of Merari brought 20 more. Additionally, 220 Nethinim (temple servants) came — all "designated by name." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Ellicott:** Suggests "a man of understanding" may be a proper name (Ishsekel), noting the "and" before Sherebiah requires this reading. The Nethinim's origin is traced here uniquely to David and the princes who appointed them to assist the Levites. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill:** Some think the Nethinim were the Gibeonites whom Joshua appointed to sanctuary service, later confirmed by David; others think these Nethinim were an additional group. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**PreceptAustin (Steven Cole):** Notes the humility of these Levites and Nethinim — though their tasks were "not as glamorous as that of the priests, they were essential if the priests were to be freed up to do their work." The 258 men and their families had very short notice to decide to return. Ezra recognized God's hand in putting it on their hearts. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

---

### v. 21 — "And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us and our children, with all our possessions."

**Traditional reading:** With the company now assembled, Ezra proclaimed a fast. The purpose was twofold: (1) to humble themselves before God, and (2) to seek a "right way" (literally "a straight way," unimpeded by obstacles and dangers) for the journey. The mention of "little ones" and "all our possessions" shows that whole families were traveling, and the treasure they carried made them targets. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Ellicott:** Notes the wilderness lay before them with "an enemy, indefinitely referred to…probably desert tribes, always lying in wait for unprotected caravans." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Historical note:** Ezra 8:21 was the text of John Robinson's last sermon at Leiden, Netherlands, before the Pilgrims sailed for the New World in 1620. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-8.html (Constable, cited in search results)

**DesiringGod (John Piper, Reformed Baptist):** Notes the connection between fasting and humbling: "Fasting is the means to humbling." Fasting says to God, "I know that I do not deserve my daily bread. My sin only deserves to be punished with starvation…I long for you, O God, vastly more than I long for food." — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-call-to-fast-for-humility-and-power

---

### v. 22 — "For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road, since we had told him, 'The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him.'"

**Traditional reading:** This is the theological heart of the chapter. Ezra had testified before the pagan king that God protects those who seek Him. To now ask for a military escort would contradict that confession and bring dishonour to God's name. Ezra was more concerned for God's glory than for his own safety. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

**Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist):** In *Morning and Evening*, Spurgeon elaborates: "A convoy on many accounts would have been desirable for the pilgrim band, but a holy shame-facedness would not allow Ezra to seek one. He feared lest the heathen king should think his professions of faith in God to be mere hypocrisy, or imagine that the God of Israel was not able to preserve his own worshippers." Spurgeon adds: "It is a most blessed thing to have no props and no buttresses, but to stand upright on the Rock of Ages, upheld by the Lord alone." He warns that "our fault seldom lies in [neglecting means]; far more frequently it springs out of foolishly believing in them instead of believing in God." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary (Spurgeon quoted at length)

**G. Campbell Morgan (cited by EnduringWord):** "The voluntary gifts of the king were welcome…It would have been quite another matter if he had asked the king to help him do what he had declared God was able to do for him." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Interesting contrast — Nehemiah's different approach:** Kidner (cited by EnduringWord) notes: "There is an added interest in the fact that Nehemiah, in his day, would see the matter quite differently, accepting a military escort as part of God's bounty (Nehemiah 2:7–9)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**PreceptAustin (Steven Cole):** Raises the thorny question: "When is it wrong to use human means in addition to trusting the Lord?" Cole answers: the normal pattern is to trust God while thankfully using the means He provides. "But sometimes using human means will lead us away from trust in the Lord, or it would be a poor witness to unbelievers. Often, this is an individual matter before the Lord." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

---

### v. 23 — "So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request."

**Traditional reading:** The fasting was not empty ritual — they "put their holy resolution into execution" (Trapp). God answered: "He was entreated of us" (Gill). The answer would be demonstrated in the safe journey recorded in v. 31. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**EnduringWord:** Notes that "real fasting — fasting that is partnered with real repentance and isn't only about image — has great power before God (Matthew 17:21)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**DesiringGod (Piper):** Connects this to 2 Chronicles 7:14 — "If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face…" — Ezra took this promise and applied it, and God heard. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-call-to-fast-for-humility-and-power

---

### vv. 24–25 — "Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests, together with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers, and I weighed out to them the contribution…"

**Traditional reading:** Ezra selected twelve priests (symbolic of the twelve tribes) and twelve Levites (Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten others) — 24 men total — and weighed out the treasure to them. The weighing before witnesses established accountability and integrity from the start. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**Ellicott:** "The gold and silver were in bars." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Notes the modern estimated value: 650 talents of silver plus 100 talents of silver articles (~$14,196,000); 100 talents of gold (~$109,200,000); plus gold basins and fine bronze (~$270,000). — From search results of https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezra-8.html

---

### vv. 26–27 — The specific items and their value

**Traditional reading:** The amounts are enormous, worth millions in modern currency. "If the God of the Jews were no more than a name…the whole exercise was pointless; but if He existed, He would expect tangible courtesies from a king — and the scale of them should reflect the donor's power and majesty" (Kidner). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Ellicott (on v. 27):** "Twenty basins of gold, of a thousand drams" — the "drams" are darics, a Persian gold coin. The "fine copper" is "probably the Roman Orichalcum, a metal very highly valued." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill (on v. 27):** Discusses the daric's value extensively, noting Bishop Cumberland's calculation that each daric weighed about twenty shillings and four pence. Suggests the fine copper may be "Corinthian brass" (a mixture of gold, silver, and copper) or Indian/Persian brass "so bright and pure, and free from rust, that it cannot be known by its colour from gold." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

---

### v. 28 — "Then I told them, 'You are holy to the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.'"

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott calls this "a unique verse in every respect." The priests and Levites were consecrated persons; the vessels and treasure were consecrated things. The holiness of both the carriers and the cargo was Ezra's ground for expecting God's protection and the men's ground for faithful stewardship. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/8-28.htm

**Pulpit Commentary:** "Since they were themselves, as priests and Levites, holy to the Lord, they were also to treat and keep the gifts committed to their charge as holy gifts." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/8-28.htm

**Gill:** The silver and gold "are a freewill offering unto the Lord God of your fathers: and therefore not to be made use of but in his service." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

---

### vv. 29–30 — "'Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem…' So the priests and Levites took charge…"

**Traditional reading:** Ezra charged them to "watch and keep" the treasure until it could be weighed again in Jerusalem before the leading priests, Levites, and family heads. This accountability structure — weighing at departure and weighing at arrival — ensured integrity on both ends and protected against both theft and false accusation. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**PreceptAustin (Cole):** Applies this to church financial integrity: "If we do not follow proper accounting procedures, it exposes workers to temptation and to accusations…We need to be scrupulous in matters of financial integrity, even on small matters." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

---

### v. 31 — "On the twelfth day of the first month we set out from the Ahava Canal to go to Jerusalem, and the hand of our God was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way."

**Traditional reading:** They departed on the 12th of Nisan (March/April), just two days before Passover began (Gill). The journey from Babylon began on the first day of the first month (Ezra 7:9); they spent about twelve days at Ahava — time used for mustering, recruiting Levites, fasting, and organizing the treasure. The entire journey took about four months. Ezra summarizes the whole trip with one theological statement: "the hand of our God was upon us." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**G. Campbell Morgan:** "God never fails those who act in full dependence on Himself, and so in complete independence of all others." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Ellicott:** "The hand of our God was upon us — This sums up the history of the journey." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

---

### v. 32 — "So we arrived at Jerusalem and rested there for three days."

**Traditional reading:** The three-day rest parallels Nehemiah's similar pause upon arrival (Nehemiah 2:11). It was a time of rest after the arduous four-month journey, and likely a time of private devotion before the public business of delivering the treasure and the king's edicts. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**Gill:** "Before they went about any business…as it was but proper they should have some rest after such a fatiguing journey." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

---

### vv. 33–34 — "On the fourth day, in the house of our God, we weighed out the silver and gold and sacred articles into the hand of Meremoth son of Uriah, the priest… Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time."

**Traditional reading:** The formal transfer of treasure took place in the temple on the fourth day. Two priests (Meremoth and Eleazar) and two Levites (Jozabad and Noadiah) received it — the same number and balance as the 24 who carried it. "Everything was verified by number and weight" — the tally matched. This proves the integrity of Ezra and his team. The written record ("all the weight was written down at that time") may have been needed to send back to the Persian court as certification. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

**EnduringWord (Yamauchi):** "According to Babylonian tradition, almost every transaction, including sales and marriages, had to be recorded in writing. Ezra may have had to send back a signed certification of the delivery of the treasures." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Ellicott:** Notes that these names of priests and Levites occur again in Nehemiah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm

---

### v. 35 — "Then the exiles who had returned from captivity sacrificed burnt offerings to the God of Israel: 12 bulls for all Israel, 96 rams, 77 lambs, and a sin offering of 12 male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD."

**Traditional reading:** Worship was the goal of the entire enterprise. The 12 bulls and 12 male goats represented all twelve tribes — even though only Judah and Benjamin were dominant, there were individuals from every tribe present (Clarke). The burnt offerings symbolized total dedication to God; the sin offerings made atonement. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Adam Clarke (Methodist):** "Though of tribes there were only Judah and Benjamin, yet they offered a bullock for every tribe, as if present. There can be little doubt that there were individuals there from all the twelve tribes, possibly some families of each." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**Gill:** The 12 bullocks and 12 he-goats were "according to the number of the tribes," and the sin offering was "to make atonement for sins they had been guilty of." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezra-8.html

**Keil & Delitzsch (cited by PreceptAustin):** "The sin-offerings availed as an atonement for the sins of all Israel, and the burnt-offerings typified the surrender of the entire nation to the service of the Lord." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-8-commentary

**Kidner (on the 77 lambs):** "The reason for offering seventy-seven lambs is not so obvious, whatever conjectures about the perfect number it may seem to invite." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

---

### v. 36 — "They also delivered the king's edicts to the royal satraps and governors of the region west of the Euphrates, who proceeded to assist the people and the house of God."

**Traditional reading:** The sequence is significant: first worship (v. 35), then the king's business. "Having rendered to God the things which were God's, they render to Caesar the things of Caesar" (Ellicott). The king's edicts were likely the documents that accredited Ezra to administer Jewish law (Ezra 7:25–26). The satraps and governors complied, providing support for both the people and the temple. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/8.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**EnduringWord (Kidner):** The king's orders were "presumably the documents that accredited Ezra as one who was authorised to administer the Jewish law among his fellow-countrymen in the various regions of the province." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

**EnduringWord (Guzik):** "This reminds us of the great purpose of Ezra's expedition…He came to give support to the people and the house of God, and only dealt with the problems of sin and compromise as necessary in the course of this greater goal." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-8/

---

## Points of Distinctive Emphasis Across Traditions

### The "Hand of God" and Divine Providence

The phrase "the hand of our God" appears three times in this chapter (vv. 18, 22, 31). **Reformed and Baptist** commentators (Gill, Spurgeon, DesiringGod/Piper) especially emphasize God's sovereign providence — that the safe journey, the recruitment of Levites, and the protection from bandits were all acts of God's sovereign hand, not human effort. The **Pentecostal/charismatic** reading (EnduringWord/Guzik) emphasises the partnership of human faith with divine power — fasting and prayer as real spiritual disciplines that "unlock" God's intervention.

### Fasting (vv. 21–23)

**Reformed Baptist (Piper/DesiringGod):** Fasting is a means to humbling, an acknowledgment that we do not deserve our daily bread. It expresses longing for God above physical pleasures. **Pentecostal/charismatic (Guzik):** Fasting has "great power before God" — a spiritual weapon that, when partnered with repentance, moves God to answer. **Evangelical (PreceptAustin/Cole):** Fasting is a practical discipline for seeking God's guidance; applicable to modern believers facing "enemies and ambushes along the way."

### Faith vs. Human Means (v. 22)

This verse is a key text for the debate on faith and practical means. **Ezra refused** a military escort on principle; **Nehemiah** later accepted one (Neh. 2:9). 

- **Spurgeon:** Strongly sides with Ezra's approach — "It is a most blessed thing to have no props and no buttresses, but to stand upright on the Rock of Ages." 
- **PreceptAustin/Cole:** Takes a balanced view: normally we trust God while using the means He provides, but sometimes using human means would be a poor witness or lead away from trust.
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Ezra's refusal was not foolhardy because "Ezra relied on God and had full confidence in Him." Asking for a guard would have meant "his faith was weak."

### The Nethinim and Lower-Status Service (vv. 15–20)

**PreceptAustin/Cole:** Highlights that "even though their jobs were not as glamorous as that of the priests, they were essential." This is applied to the church: "all the parts of the body of Christ are necessary for the proper functioning of the whole."

### Male Leadership (v. 1 list)

**PreceptAustin/Cole:** Makes a point about male headship: "Ezra knew the structure of his society well enough to direct his appeal to the heads of families, knowing that in most cases if they came they would bring their groups with them." Applies this to church leadership structures, arguing elders should be male per New Testament qualifications.
